articles.title: Explaining the difference between brittle and ductile behavior in polymer glasses
articles.dek: Glasses are (mostly) brittle, metals can be ductile (plastic), and liquids flow easily.
paragraphs: Glasses are (mostly) brittle, metals can be ductile (plastic), and liquids flow easily. Polymers are interesting because they exhibit all three types of behavior, depending on their chemical nature, temperature, and deformation rate. If polymers are not able to crystallize, their low-temperature state is glassy, and they are hard and transparent. One example is poly(methylmethacrylate) [PMMA], which has been used as an artificial glass since the early 20th century.

Surprisingly, polymer glasses can be ductile at temperatures significantly below their glass transition temperature, T g . For a typical laboratory strain rate (~10⁻³ s⁻¹), the brittle-ductile transition temperature (BDT or T BD ) can be 50–100 K below T g . This result is surprising—naively, one would expect a "glass" to be brittle—yet polymers can deform plastically well below T g .

In collaboration with Profs. Oleg Gendelman (Technion, Israel) and Alessio Zaccone (University of Milan, Italy), I started by developing a simple model that captures the main features of the three types of stress-strain behavior: brittle (Type I), ductile with stress overshoot (Type II), and ductile with no stress overshoot (Type III).

For more than a century, scientists have studied viscoelastic materials using simplified representations like the Maxwell element (spring and dashpot connected in series). Our model—now published in Soft Matter —is based on that Maxwell element, but with two big modifications. First, the elastic component is not a pure linear spring, but a sinusoidal function of the elastic strain, reflecting the fact that the potential energy landscape has multiple minima. Second, the dashpot viscosity decreases at large strains, as predicted by the so-called Eyring-Long model.

With our model, we can calculate the yield strain corresponding to each strain rate. For small strain rates, the yield strain is small, and the stress-strain curve is of Type III. For intermediate strain rates, the yield strain is larger, and the stress-strain curve is of Type II. Finally, for large strain rates, there is no solution, the material does not flow, and the stress-strain curve is of Type I.

We thus look at the brittle-ductile transition differently from earlier researchers. In our view, a polymer glass can yield uniformly if the strain rate is slower than a temperature-dependent threshold but must break in a brittle fashion if the strain rate is faster than that threshold. How can we compute this threshold? Our hypothesis is that this threshold is inversely proportional to the Johari-Goldstein beta-relaxation time. (This idea was formulated empirically by Dr. S. Wu (Dupont) in the 1970s, but we are now able to come up with a theoretical justification. )

In the undeformed state, the relaxation time is large (alpha-relaxation time), and, as the material is deformed, it decreases all the way down to the beta-relaxation time. Knowing the two relaxation times as a function of temperature, we can then compute the BDT as a function of the strain rate.

Crucially, the alpha-relaxation time in glassy polymers depends on the aging of the polymer; at temperatures far below T g , it seldom reaches equilibrium and is generally on the order of the aging time. Thus, the analysis of the BDT requires knowledge of the sample age—a fact known to experimentalists but often underappreciated by theoreticians.

From the model, we can get the "universal" map separating the three regions: brittle, ductile with stress overshoot, and ductile with no stress overshoot (see figure below). The x-axis is proportional to the logarithm of the ratio of the alpha- and beta-relaxation times—or, alternatively, the inverse of the absolute temperature. The y-axis represents normalized strain rate. Hence, we see that at high temperatures (small B), only liquid-like (at small strain rates) or brittle (at large strain rates) behaviors are possible.

Knowing the temperature dependence of the alpha- and beta-relaxation times for several amorphous polymers, we can translate the "universal" phase map into polymer-specific BDT results. For PMMA, the comparison between the model and experiment was plotted in the top figure. In the paper, we also show similar plots for poly(vinylchloride) [PVC] and polystyrene [PS]. For all three polymers, the model fit is within 5 K of the experimental data.

articles.title: NASA Welcomes Vietnam as Newest Artemis Accords Signatory
articles.dek: The Socialist Republic of Vietnam became the 78th nation to sign the Artemis Accords, joining a growing coalition of like-minded nations committed to the peaceful,…
paragraphs: The Socialist Republic of Vietnam became the 78th nation to sign the Artemis Accords, joining a growing coalition of like-minded nations committed to the peaceful, transparent, and responsible exploration of space.

“Vietnam is joining at an important point in the development of its own space program,” said NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson in recorded remarks for the ceremony. “NASA and the Vietnam National Space Center have built momentum in satellite innovation, land-use research, and radar-based Earth observation. Joining the Artemis Accords opens a new chapter in that relationship. We’ve aligned on the principles. The opportunities are in front of us, and now we can build on that foundation together. We are proud to welcome Vietnam to the Artemis Accords community.”

Vietnam’s Minister of Science and Technology Vũ Hải Quân signed the Artemis Accords on behalf of the country during the Vietnam International Digital Week in Ha Long. The United States Ambassador to Vietnam Jennifer Wicks also participated in the signing event.

Vietnam’s decision extends the U. S. -Vietnam Comprehensive Strategic Partnership into a new frontier. Built on more than 30 years of cooperation, the partnership spans defense, economic, law enforcement, war legacy, and technological cooperation, and it advances peace, stability, and prosperity in a free and open Indo-Pacific.

Earlier this year, NASA partnered with Vietnam’s Vietnamese-German University to support the agency’s Soil Moisture Active Passive mission, which measures surface-soil water worldwide. Vietnam also inaugurated its National Space Center in Hanoi and is developing domestic satellite capabilities through the LOTUSat program, focusing on Earth observation, weather monitoring, and disaster response.

In 2020, NASA and the State Department joined with seven other founding nations to establish the Artemis Accords, responding to the growing interest in lunar activities by both governments and private companies. They introduced the first set of practical principles aimed at enhancing the safety and coordination between nations as they explore the Moon, Mars, and beyond.

Signing the Artemis Accords means committing to explore peaceably and transparently, to render aid to those in need, to enable access to scientific data that all of humanity can learn from, to ensure activities do not interfere with those of others, and to preserve historically significant sites and artifacts by developing best practices for space exploration for the benefit of all.
More countries are expected to sign the Artemis Accords in the months and years ahead, as NASA continues its work to establish a safe, peaceful, and prosperous future in space.

articles.title: Q&A: Decoding the cell—a conversation with a computational biologist
articles.dek: Computational biologist Christina Leslie, Ph. D. , has spent nearly two decades at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK) building computational tools that help make…
paragraphs: Computational biologist Christina Leslie, Ph. D. , has spent nearly two decades at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK) building computational tools that help make sense of some of the most complex data in biology.

Today, Leslie's work sits at the crossroads of two technological revolutions. Single-cell genomics is allowing scientists to probe the activation of genes in individual cells, revealing the distinct roles, identities, and behaviors of every cell type in a tissue or tumor. Meanwhile, the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) is making it possible to find meaningful patterns in complex single-cell data sets at a scale far beyond more traditional computational methods.

Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center sat down with Leslie to discuss the promise—and limitations—of this frontier, and how these advances could help researchers design better therapies, decode why tumors resist treatment, and tailor treatments to each individual and their unique cancer.

The theme of my lab, which is in MSK's Sloan Kettering Institute, is studying how gene expression is regulated in mammalian cells—including in the immune system and in cancer. We use tools from what used to be called machine learning and is now called artificial intelligence.
In the past few years, we've been using AI to analyze three increasingly powerful types of biological data.
AI gives us the computational power to make sense of all three of these complex data types and to find the patterns within them that would otherwise be invisible.

Single-cell genomics is an increasingly important way that we make new discoveries in biology. Before, we would do what's known as "bulk" analysis, which allowed us to look at what was happening in a tissue sample—but with the molecular data from all the cells mixed together. Now, we have ways of barcoding individual cells in a sample so that we can understand how cells play different functional roles in a particular system. And we can discover new cell types and functional specializations.
Let me give you two examples from recent work done at MSK:

We collaborated with Dr. Chrysothemis Brown using single-cell approaches to discover a new specialized type of immune cell called Thetis cells, which help explain how the immune system learns to tolerate food and helpful gut bacteria early in life. This work is shedding new light on childhood food allergies.

We also worked with the lab of Dr. Alexander Rudensky, who heads MSK's Immunology Program, to uncover that there are two distinct types of regulatory T cells at work in colorectal cancer —IL-10 positive and IL-10 negative—which play completely opposite roles in tumor progression. One promotes tumor growth while the other restrains it—which highlights the need to develop therapies that can selectively eliminate the harmful cells while preserving the helpful ones. We wouldn't have been able to differentiate between these two subpopulations of cells without single-cell techniques.

Data sets generated by these technologies are quite large—some single-cell atlases are now 150 million cells—so you need more sophisticated tools to make sense of them.

The AI community adapted models from natural language processing and computer vision for single-cell data relatively early on. And there's real logic to that—you have a lot of data, you need to find patterns, and these tools are powerful.

But cells, genomes, and expression profiles are not natural language and they're not images. If you just directly take these models and say, "OK, we have a bunch of genes, so let's treat them like words"—that's not quite right. Genes aren't organized in a sentence. There is an underlying structure, which is the structure of gene regulation. When cells receive specific signals from the body, they turn on sets of genes in a coordinated way. And that biology needs to be represented in our models.

articles.title: Chornobyl dog population shows genetic signatures of directional selection
articles.dek: The latest research on the wild population of dogs in Chornobyl reveals that the genetic differences between these dogs and other similarly isolated dog populations are…
paragraphs: The latest research on the wild population of dogs in Chornobyl reveals that the genetic differences between these dogs and other similarly isolated dog populations are likely evidence of directional selection, not mutation. The work suggests a potential association between genetic selection and environmental variables and could advance understanding of local adaptation and genomic resilience in contaminated environments. The study appears in Genes .

Previously, researchers had looked at genetic differences in two populations of dogs: one located at the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant (NPP) and the other in Chornobyl City, approximately 10 miles (16 kilometers) away. They found that the genetics of Chornobyl City dogs were very similar to dog populations in Russia, Poland and the surrounding areas, whereas those from the NPP had some distinct differences—specifically in regions associated with DNA repair.

"This work ties up some of the loose ends from our previous work, where in characterizing the population's genetic structure we found that while these two dog groups are geographically very close, they have a very high degree of genetic difference, and those differences aren't due to mutation," said Megan Dillon, a postdoctoral research scholar at North Carolina State University's College of Veterinary Medicine.

"With this work we wanted to explore two additional larger-scale evolutionary drivers—are the genetic differences due to selection, or are they due to genetic drift over time in an isolated population?"

Through natural selection, genes that increase an individual's environmental fitness become more prevalent in a population over time. Directional selection is a more notable type of natural selection in which an entire population shifts toward a small number of favored traits over time. Directional selection is typically associated with environmental changes.

Genetic drift refers to random genetic changes not necessarily associated with fitness that nonetheless become common in a population. Genetic drift is more prevalent in small, isolated populations because the likelihood of those random changes being passed down is greater and can result in reduced genome-wide diversity.

The research team compared the genomic data of the two Chornobyl populations with that of free-breeding dogs from Eastern Europe and with an isolated dog population from the Galápagos Islands, to try and tease out the effects of isolation versus environment on the NPP dogs.

While the effective population size of the NPP population is small, it didn't differ significantly from that of the Chornobyl City population. The NPP also didn't show evidence of reduced genetic variation consistent with genetic drift.

Genetically, the NPP population differed significantly from other geographically isolated dog populations, including those from the Galápagos Islands. In contrast, the dog population in Chornobyl City was found to be genetically more similar to dog populations in the Galápagos Islands than to the nearby NPP population.

Finally, genomic analysis of the NPP dogs identified evidence of directional selection at over 100 locations. The genes located around these loci are associated with cancer development, DNA replication and repair, cell cycle functions and immune function.

"While we can't say for certain whether what we've found can be directly confirmed as selection, we do find these genomic signatures suggestive of selection," Dillon said. "When we dig deeper into those genomic regions, we find that these genes are involved in biologically relevant pathways that could allow them to overcome the effects of being exposed to toxicants in this environment."

articles.title: Could next-gen artificial intelligence help map out future space outposts?
articles.dek: Planning a successful trip can be challenging, especially when your destination is in outer space.
paragraphs: Planning a successful trip can be challenging, especially when your destination is in outer space. Even before liftoff, space missions require extraordinary amounts of scientific preparation and data analysis to succeed, which can take years to complete. However, as space agencies race to establish a permanent presence on the moon, using artificial intelligence to combine such information into a single system could make mission planning much more efficient.

One such system, developed by Gokce Inal, a Ph. D. candidate in civil, environmental and geodetic engineering at The Ohio State University, is an AI framework designed to help scientists evaluate potential lunar landing sites, identify dangerous hazards future crews might face, and scour new regions for scientifically valuable geologic features.

"AI systems are going to become critical tools for space exploration that will help humans analyze the millions of images and data sets that future missions will require," she said. "This work is meant to serve as a bridge between those two worlds, AI and planetary science."

Landing on the moon is more difficult today than it ever was, but preliminary results from Inal's model, dubbed "LUMINA," show a strong ability to make complex lunar observations as well as generate scientifically meaningful mission commentary for candidate landing sites. Such capabilities could help mission planners locate areas abundant with water ice and other resources.

Built on a previously developed lunar vision-language foundation model called LLaVA-LE that could describe lunar terrain and answer scientific questions, LUMINA extends the team's research by using a framework that can plan and carry out multistep analyses, evaluate potential lunar landing sites and explain the evidence behind its recommendations, said Inal.

While she created LUMINA to advance lunar mission objectives, Inal envisions the AI model not as a semiautonomous machine, but as a decision-support system designed to work in tandem with mission planners to make final judgments. "Most AI tools are passive tools," she said. "You ask a question and get an answer, but we're moving toward an active scientific assistant that can work through a problem alongside the experts."
Inal presented her findings this month at The 58th Annual Meeting of the Division for Planetary Sciences ( DPS 58 ) of the American Astronomical Society.

One of this work's main goals is to establish a pathway for agentic systems to be used in support of future space exploration, but LUMINA's capabilities extend beyond only data interpretation for the lunar surface. Instead, the model could have research and exploration applications for mapping the surface of many other planetary bodies, including Earth, said Alper Yilmaz, co-author of the research and a professor in civil, environmental and geodetic engineering at Ohio State.

"There aren't many GPT-like map models being developed for space exploration, so our effort is aimed at making one generalizable to other surfaces, like Mars or some asteroids," he said.

As new data sets become more advanced, more efficient tools like this model will be needed to help mission planners search them—otherwise trying to discern the best places for future crews to land or investigate would be like looking for a needle in a haystack, said Yilmaz.
"People are going to be landing in an extremely harsh environment, so it's worth having another set of eyes that can verify and question things and help us communicate better," he said.
As the system continues to develop, the team plans to test it on new high-quality lunar data and further evaluate how well it supports mission planning.

"NASA's Artemis program creates important opportunities for our research," she said. "As new lunar data becomes available, their results can improve systems like ours and better support future mission planning."

articles.title: Same radical, different paths: X-ray snapshots reveal how neighboring molecules shape its movement
articles.dek: Chemical reactions have their own "impatient molecules." Unable to stay still even for a moment, they latch onto other molecules indiscriminately.
paragraphs: Chemical reactions have their own "impatient molecules." Unable to stay still even for a moment, they latch onto other molecules indiscriminately. Researchers have now found that even these molecules change where they "sit" and how far they roam depending on who their neighbors are. The findings are expected to help scientists make better medicines and materials by directing reactions only to the desired sites.

A research team led by Professor Kyung Hwan Kim of the Department of Chemistry at Pohang University of Science and Technology, in collaboration with Professor Seung Jun Hwang's team in the Department of Chemistry at KAIST, captured the first encounters between radicals and neighboring molecules on a timescale of one 10 billionth of a second, or 100 picoseconds.

The team found that the structure of the neighboring molecule changes where a radical resides and the range over which it moves. The study was published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society .

Where a single atom attaches can make a substantial difference to a drug's effectiveness or a material's performance, much as where a LEGO brick is placed changes what gets built. This is why "selectivity"—directing reactions to the desired sites—is important in developing new drugs and functional materials.

Radicals are molecules with unpaired electrons. They are useful for forming new bonds, but their high reactivity makes them difficult to control. Researchers have known that changing the environment around a catalyst can alter reaction outcomes. Yet these encounters were too fleeting to observe how neighboring molecules influence where radicals reside and in which directions they move.

The team focused on the "first contact," when a radical and a neighboring molecule briefly stay close to one another just before a bond forms. They used time-resolved X-ray solution scattering (TR-XSS), a technique that captures molecular motion in a series of snapshots separated by extremely short intervals. Much as a high-speed camera captures a bullet in flight frame by frame, the technique records fleeting molecular moments in successive snapshots.

At a synchrotron facility of the High Energy Accelerator Research Organization (KEK) in Japan, the team prepared separate solutions of molecular iodine in benzene and mesitylene. Laser pulses split the iodine molecules to generate radicals, and X-rays probed the solutions after controlled time delays. The measurements showed that "contact complexes," in which radicals come into close contact with neighboring molecules, had already formed just 100 picoseconds later.

The radicals behaved very differently in the two solvents. In benzene, which has a hexagonal ring, the radical occupied positions near the ring's edge and rapidly moved around its perimeter, as if riding a carousel. In mesitylene, where three small side branches called "methyl groups" are attached to the benzene ring, the radical instead favored a direction without a side branch and moved only within a narrow range.

Benzene was like "open seating," where any seat is available, while mesitylene was like "assigned seating," where each seat is fixed. A small difference in the neighboring molecule's structure changed not only the radical's preferred position but also the "paths" it could take.

The study presents a perspective on radical reactions that considers not only how stably a radical is held, but also where it resides and in which directions it moves. By carefully designing the surrounding environment, researchers can guide radicals to desired sites so that only the intended reactions take place.
The findings are expected to lay the groundwork for synthetic strategies that enable more precise production of effective new drugs and high-performance materials.

"The significance of this study is that we moved beyond inferring reaction processes from their final products to directly identifying the structure of a short-lived contact state between a radical and a neighboring molecule," said Professor Kim. "We expect that extending this work to reactants used in practical synthesis will help us design molecular environments that guide desired reactions."

articles.title: Schools increasingly affected by poor air quality as wildfire smoke becomes more common
articles.dek: American children are increasingly exposed to air pollution as wildfire smoke becomes more common, and some schools and child care centers struggle to keep indoor breathing…
paragraphs: American children are increasingly exposed to air pollution as wildfire smoke becomes more common, and some schools and child care centers struggle to keep indoor breathing conditions clean, a new national study shows.

The researchers note that components of wildfire smoke, including PM 2. 5 , which is fine particulate matter with a diameter of 2. 5 micrometers or smaller, are known health hazards, especially for adolescents and younger children.

For the study, published in Environmental Research , scientists looked at air quality data from across the United States from 2006 through 2023 and found some alarming trends, said co-author Molly Kile of Oregon State University.

"The average number of annual smoke days at public schools rose from 6. 8 to 54. 4 between the beginning and end of the study period," said Kile, an environmental epidemiologist in the OSU College of Health. "Child care centers experienced an increase from 9. 4 to 112. 2 days. Our children are collectively experiencing billions of days of smoky air each year."

Four decades of data from the National Interagency Fire Center show that the number of U. S. wildfires per year has remained relatively stable—generally in the range of 70,000—but the intensity of those fires and the acreage burned have increased.
And while the western part of the country tends to see more fires and heavier smoke, the issue is a national one, Kile emphasizes.

"Yes, there is more severe wildfire smoke in the West, but fine particulate matter travels hundreds and thousands of miles," she said. "And the prevailing wind blows from west to east, so it all goes downwind."
PM 2. 5 can be inhaled deeply into the lungs and even enter the bloodstream, is a known cause of cardiovascular disease and is linked to the onset and worsening of respiratory illness.

As climate change exacerbates wildfire risk , PM 2. 5 emissions from fires have surged to the point that wildfires now account for almost half of all PM 2. 5 across the United States and have negated air quality improvements in multiple regions.

"We are often told to stay indoors when air pollution gets severe but being indoors does not guarantee clean air," Kile said, noting that indoor air quality measurements showed substantial variation in how well buildings protected occupants from outdoor fine particulate pollution.

"Some schools had higher indoor PM 2. 5 concentrations than nearby outdoor measurements during smoke days," she said. "This is a particularly actionable finding and emphasizes the need for investment in improving indoor air quality in schools through HVAC upgrades, which can be expensive, or portable HEPA filters , which can be a more affordable approach."

Stephanie Foster, the study's corresponding author, notes that because of the amount of time students spend in schools and child care centers, those places are important settings for safeguarding children's health.

"We found that the buildings where children spend much of their day do not consistently protect them from air pollution," said Foster, scholarly activity program manager in Samaritan Health Services' Research Development Office. "But educational facilities are places where coordinated preparedness plans, air filtration, indoor air quality monitoring and changes to activities during smoke events could reduce exposure."
Joining Foster and Kile on the study were Andrew Larkin, Megan MacDonald, Megan McClelland and Perry Hystad of the OSU College of Health and Parichehr Salimifard of the OSU College of Engineering.

articles.title: No Batteries, No Plugs: Scientists Create a Tiny Sensor That Powers Itself
articles.dek: Scientists have developed a tiny temperature sensor that harvests energy from magnetic fields near electrical wiring.
paragraphs: Scientists have developed a tiny temperature sensor that harvests energy from magnetic fields near electrical wiring.

Electrical wiring produces weak electromagnetic fields that typically go unnoticed, but researchers have found a way to turn some of that energy into a power source for tiny electronic devices. Scientists at the University of Arkansas (U of A) and the University of Michigan have developed a graphene-based energy harvester capable of powering an ultra-low-power temperature sensor without a conventional battery.

The prototype operates using energy collected from its immediate surroundings, consuming power measured in nanowatts, or billionths of a watt. It represents another advance toward the team’s goal of developing autonomous sensors that could function unattended for decades.

The technology captures energy from magnetic fields generated by electrical wiring carrying alternating current. In the United States, electricity typically operates at 60 hertz, meaning the current changes direction 60 times each second. The researchers designed their sensor to harvest energy from these low-frequency fields.

A graphene inductor collects the energy and sends an alternating electrical signal to a custom circuit, which converts it into direct current. That electricity charges capacitors that store energy for the sensor to use. Unlike a battery, a capacitor stores energy in an electric field rather than through chemical reactions.

“The inductor adds charge to these capacitors at a slow rate,” explained University of Arkansas physics professor Paul Thibado, “but it’s faster than the rate the sensor uses up the charges from the capacitors.”

Because the sensor consumes energy more slowly than the system replenishes it, the capacitors can maintain an electrical reserve. Thibado estimates that this stored energy could keep the device operating for at least 24 hours during a power outage, potentially extending to a week.

The new device is the second graphene-powered temperature sensor developed by the research team. Their earlier work demonstrated that graphene-based solar cells could supply enough electricity to operate temperature sensors, establishing another possible source of energy for autonomous electronics.

Graphene, a material consisting of a single layer of carbon atoms, has electrical properties that make it useful in energy-harvesting technologies. Thibado has investigated these properties for more than a decade and invented the graphene energy harvesters used in the team’s research.

The researchers ultimately want to combine several methods of collecting environmental energy, including sunlight, heat, sound, motion, and ambient electromagnetic fields. A sensor equipped with multiple harvesting systems could continue operating when one energy source becomes unavailable, reducing its dependence on any single power supply.

Although temperature measurement provides a practical demonstration, the technology could eventually support sensors used in agriculture, environmental monitoring, medical tracking, wearable electronics, and supply chain management. These applications often require devices to operate in locations where replacing batteries is expensive, inconvenient, or impractical.

Thibado describes the long-term vision as “set it and forget it,” with sensors designed to operate for extended periods without routine battery replacement. Eliminating disposable batteries could also reduce maintenance demands and electronic waste, although decades of reliable operation have not yet been demonstrated.

The research was published in the Journal of Vacuum Science and Technology B , with MD Rezaul Kabir, a doctoral candidate in materials science and engineering at the University of Arkansas, serving as first author. The project also involves researchers at the University of Michigan, including electrical engineering and computer science professor David Blaauw, whose work focuses on low-power wireless sensors and embedded systems.

NTS Innovations, a nanotechnology company, holds the exclusive license to commercialize the graphene energy-harvesting technology. The company has supported patent development, business planning, and efforts to identify potential customers and commercial partners.

articles.title: Artemis III SLS Core Stage Joins Boosters at Kennedy
articles.dek: NASA’s Artemis III SLS (Space Launch System) core stage is integrated alongside the twin solid rocket boosters on Oct.
paragraphs: NASA’s Artemis III SLS (Space Launch System) core stage is integrated alongside the twin solid rocket boosters on Oct. 28 inside the Vehicle Assembly Building’s High Bay 3 at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

Technicians lifted the 212-foot rocket stage from the facility’s High Bay 2 using a one-of-a kind lifting beam designed to place the stage onto the mobile launcher. Once testing and checkouts are complete, teams will roll the core stage and booster stack out to Launch Pad 39B to conduct a tanking test where liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen fuel will be loaded only into the core stage and launch teams will practice countdown procedures and timelines.

The Artemis III mission will launch NASA astronauts Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio, Andre Douglas, and ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Luca Parmitano in the Orion spacecraft on top of the SLS rocket to test rendezvous and docking capabilities between Orion and commercial spacecraft from Blue Origin and SpaceX ahead of future mission to land astronauts on the Moon.

articles.title: 3 major issues that Republican Byron Donalds or Democrat David Jolly will need to address as Florida’s next governor
articles.dek: After nearly three decades of Republican control of Florida, the executive office of the governor has become more powerful than ever before.
paragraphs: After nearly three decades of Republican control of Florida, the executive office of the governor has become more powerful than ever before.
So when Florida voters choose between Republican Byron Donalds and Democrat David Jolly for governor on Nov. 3, the winner will be poised to shape the state’s direction for years to come.

I’m a political scientist who has lived in Florida for almost two decades and seen the powers of the governor’s office grow. I’ve been watching how the two candidates say they will use their authority to shape policy around healthcare, education and home rule – and what help they might need from the Legislature.

One of the first choices awaiting the new governor will be whom to appoint as Florida surgeon general, a position created in 2007 . The surgeon general oversees the Florida Department of Health and county health departments across the state.

The position comes with the power to declare public health emergencies , forcibly quarantine people and set vaccine mandates for illnesses such as chickenpox that fall outside the state Legislature’s framework of seven childhood vaccine mandates .

As part of his conservative remake of Florida policies , Gov. Ron DeSantis appointed the current surgeon general, Dr. Joseph Ladapo , to the position in 2021. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Ladapo emerged as a leading medical freedom advocate and vaccine skeptic.

Ladapo opposes all vaccine mandates . At the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, he recommended against COVID-19 vaccinations for healthy children and ended quarantine mandates for Florida public schoolchildren exposed to COVID-19. He also said that he wanted mRNA vaccines “not to be available to anyone” in the state.

Ladapo also proposed new Florida health rules in October 2026 to drop mandates for four vaccines required for school attendance, including chickenpox and hepatitis B. Currently, the state allows exemptions only for approved religious or medical reasons.
The Florida Chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics opposes the rule change on public health grounds.

Donalds has long opposed vaccine mandates and says that he did not personally receive a COVID-19 vaccine . He supports Ladapo’s proposed rule change to reduce school vaccination mandates and says he is open to reappointing Ladapo as surgeon general.

Jolly, on the other hand, supports Florida’s current school vaccine mandates and exemptions . He says he would fire Ladapo on Day 1 in favor of someone who “ embraces science and evidence-based public health .”

No matter which candidate is elected governor, the Florida Legislature has tied his hands on how far he can push vaccine policy. The Legislature has mandated measles and polio vaccines for all K-12 public school students, so getting rid of that requirement would require a change in the law. It also stripped the surgeon general of the power to enforce vaccine mandates during public health emergencies in November 2021, during the pandemic.

One of the biggest developments in Florida K-12 education in recent years has been the creation of a system of universal vouchers by DeSantis and the Legislature in 2023. This program allows parents of any income level to use US$8,000 in state money on average, based on county of residence , for their children’s private or homeschooling education.

The universal voucher program has created intense pressure on the state budget. It cost an estimated $4. 5 billion in fiscal year 2026 . State auditors have identified accountability problems in tracking funds through the system. Public schools have faced declining enrollment , with fewer resources to serve the neediest students they cannot turn away.

Donalds strongly supports the universal voucher program, recounting how his family saved money for him to attend a private high school . Donalds has touted universal vouchers in Christian nationalist circles and expressed an interest in making Florida “ the model state for school choice ” by allowing parents to choose among private educational providers competing in the marketplace .
His wife, Erika Donalds, is a former Collier County school board member who operates a network of for-profit charter schools and advocates nationally for school choice .

The only change Donalds has proposed is a universal scorecard for the voucher program so that parents can compare educational data on student performance across different types of schools. Currently, only public schools must provide this data.

Jolly also supports the universal voucher program but wants significant changes. Jolly personally sends his own two children to private, faith-based schools with the support of vouchers . He says private schools that accept vouchers should meet the same standards and requirements as public schools , including the mandate to serve students with disabilities. He also wants to limit private school tuition to the value of the voucher and reinstate benefit eligibility based on financial need .
Campaign promises aside, neither candidate can do much to affect the universal voucher program, because it was created by the Legislature.

Democrat Jolly knows he would need the Legislature’s cooperation to advance reforms and claims that he has identified Republican allies to do so. Donalds would likely face a friendly Republican majority for his more modest proposed reforms.

The next Florida governor will also be able to influence state education policy by appointing the seven members of the Board of Education and then recommending a candidate for commissioner of education for that board to elect. The commissioner and state board oversee the Florida Department of Education and programs from kindergarten through postsecondary education.
The position of commissioner used to be elected, but in 2002 voters approved a constitutional amendment creating the current system, which gives more power to the governor.

The next governor’s appointees to the Board of Education could try to shape the effects of universal vouchers more indirectly. The board could approve an annual legislative budget request with new recommended funding levels for public education to make up for shortfalls due to revenue loss from vouchers.
They could also implement new eligibility rules for private school vouchers, as the DeSantis administration has done .

articles.title: Experts Spent Decades Searching for the Secret to Happiness. Here’s What They Found
articles.dek: Some of the world’s leading happiness researchers have changed how they live because of what they have discovered.
paragraphs: Some of the world’s leading happiness researchers have changed how they live because of what they have discovered. After decades of studying well-being, several have made a conscious effort to spend more time with family and friends, reflecting one of the strongest findings in happiness science.

Their insights come from a discussion involving 13 international experts with a combined 600 years of research experience. The conversation, which explored both scientific evidence and personal experience, led to a new paper published in the Journal of Happiness Studies .

“Happiness emerges from a symphony of factors, but if I had to pinpoint one secret to happiness, relationships with other people might be it,” says Lara Aknin, a professor of social psychology at Simon Fraser University.

Aknin coauthored the paper with Harvard University’s Säde Stenlund and Kelsey O’Connor, a senior researcher at Luxembourg’s National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies. She emphasizes that social connections are among the most consistently supported findings in happiness research.
“Having relationships is one of the most reliable predictors of happiness that has emerged from a robust body of evidence spanning the social sciences,” says Aknin.
“We know that having just one person you can count on is extremely consequential. Having more relationships and more communities that you feel a part of compounds that sense of well-being.”

Although genetics and life circumstances influence happiness, researchers emphasize that well-being is not necessarily fixed. People who generally consider themselves happy still experience setbacks, stress, and negative emotions. Their overall well-being can depend partly on how they respond to challenges and the activities they choose to pursue.

Some influential models of happiness have estimated that life circumstances, including where someone lives, employment, age, and relationship status, account for roughly 10% of happiness, while voluntary activities may contribute as much as 40%. These figures are model-based estimates rather than fixed proportions that apply to everyone, but they highlight the potential role of personal behavior.

“That leaves a lot of opportunity for people who may be more innately pessimistic to start practising research-backed strategies like meditation or gratitude that might help them see the world in a more positive way,” she says.

The scientific study of well-being has expanded considerably since the 1970s, when the modern field began taking shape. What was once a relatively small area of research now encompasses numerous approaches to understanding happiness, life satisfaction, social relationships, and psychological health.

Aknin, who also coedits the annual World Happiness Report , says this expansion has brought challenges. As researchers pursue increasingly specialized questions, some early leaders worry that the field has become fragmented. Despite these differences, the scientists who participated in the discussion shared a commitment to rigorous research that can be translated into practical ways to improve people’s lives.

The researchers also considered how personal well-being affects people’s willingness and ability to support others. Studies have linked happiness with positive outcomes beyond individual life satisfaction, including greater motivation to help other people.

“With many large and threatening realities taking place in the world right now, I sometimes worry that the pursuit of happiness can seem trite. But one reason I remain committed to the scientific study of happiness is that happiness in and of itself predicts a number of valuable outcomes, including the motivation to help other people,” she explains.
“When people feel they are doing well, they have the ability, the capability, and the motivation to engage in world affairs—to take care of the people they love and take care of their communities.”

articles.title: NASA University Challenge Ignites Trajectory of Drone Entrepreneur
articles.dek: Five years ago, Gavin Gardner was a Michigan State University engineering student researching next-generation drone technology as part of a NASA grant.
paragraphs: Five years ago, Gavin Gardner was a Michigan State University engineering student researching next-generation drone technology as part of a NASA grant. Garder expected the research to be demanding – but he was surprised that navigating the financial side of the work presented an even greater challenge.

Although Gardner was used to leading fellow students in a lab setting, he and his team were completely new to things like creating budgets, handling large sums of money, and promoting their work for crowdfunding.

That’s why demonstrating both engineering and entrepreneurship skills are major tentpoles of NASA’s University Student Research Challenge (USRC), an initiative that provides grants to teams of college students interested in helping the agency realize its aeronautical research goals.

“Half the battle is building your product,” Gardner said recently. “The other half is selling the product in a way that everyone else can understand what you’re doing and not talking in nerdy, engineering ways.”

Gardner and his Michigan State USRC alumni teammates are still using those lessons today, as aerospace developers. In 2024, they founded their own company, AG3 Labs, which specializes in drones for military training exercises.

“I don’t think I would discredit our technical expertise in getting us to where we are today, but I know that USRC was a booster that really amplified our trajectory at such a young age,” Gardner said.

NASA USRC manager Steven Holz said Gardner’s experience shows what students can accomplish when they receive both a grant and guidance – enabling a future workforce and contributing to the aviation industry.

“We are proud to see the success of USRC alumni,” Holz said. “We hope that every team that participates in the program sees, like Gavin, how they can grow technically, entrepreneurially, and use the opportunity as a launchpad for their own innovative careers.”
Gardner’s path to running his own company began with a middle school age trip to Space Camp, where he began realizing that he wanted to be an engineer.
The engineering bug also bit his brother, Gryson Gardner, and the two of them would often be found in their Michigan garage tinkering with various machinery, including drones and electronic kits.

When Gardner arrived at Michigan State, he looked for extracurricular groups and found one dedicated to the increasingly popular hobby of drones. He gained hands-on, practical experience in how drones are made and operated.

In 2021, Gardner received an email from a friend who told him they had just won a USRC grant from NASA for an activity called Aerial Intra-city Delivery Electric Drones (AIDED), and they needed help building a new drone.
“We had this idea that instead of flying through the whole city, why can’t a drone just hitchhike a ride on a city bus like everyone else does?” Gardner said.

The concept was for a cargo-carrying drone to take off, dock on top of public transportation such as a bus, charge its batteries while riding along, and then take off for its final leg of the delivery. The team built and flew a full-scale drone to prove the concept but decided against pursuing a commercial venture.

articles.title: NASA Selects 19 New Citizen Science Proposals in 2026
articles.dek: So far, 2026 has seen a flood of successes for volunteers who do NASA science, exemplifying NASA’s commitment to gold-standard science—transparent, reproducible and…
paragraphs: So far, 2026 has seen a flood of successes for volunteers who do NASA science, exemplifying NASA’s commitment to gold-standard science—transparent, reproducible and intrinsically collaborative. The Backyard Worlds: Planet 9 project announced that their project volunteers have now discovered most of the known brown dwarfs , celestial objects that are similar to planets. The Zooniverse platform, with grant from NASA, reached a milestone of 1 billion classifications. Several projects have come online that leverage new super intelligence (SI) techniques to amplify or extend the work of volunteers. More NASA volunteers are using SI to build their own data tools and help write scientific papers than ever before.

Even with all of those achievements, our science community is already working on the next round of new volunteer projects and innovations. NASA’s Science Mission Directorate has selected nineteen proposals from research teams in 2026 that will result in new opportunities for you to do NASA science.

The Citizen Science Seed Funding Program (CSSFP-25) of NASA’s Science Mission Directorate aims to support scientists and other experts to develop citizen science projects and expand the pool of professional scientists who use citizen science techniques in their science investigations. Twelve new proposals to this program were selected.

“The Rogue Worlds Project: Activating volunteers to uncover the hidden population of super Jupiters with SPHEREx” led by Principal Investigator Jacqueline Faherty from the American Museum of Natural History. This project will invite you to search data from NASA’s SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer) mission to find free-floating planets and brown dwarfs in clusters of young stars. The SPHEREx space observatory mapping the entire sky in near-infrared wavelengths.

“ Quantifying the calibrations between intrinsic galaxy merger timescales with visual pair/tidal-feature classifications” led by Principal Investigator Kameswara Bharadwaj Mantha of the University of Missouri. This project will investigate galaxy mergers, helping astronomers understand how galaxies evolve through time. You will be invited to classify realistic mock images of galaxies to help probe the statistics and dynamical evolution of galaxy mergers.

“ Overlap Zoo; cosmic light tables for galaxy transparency” led by Principal Investigator Benne Holwerda of the University of Louisville. Galaxies, which glow with the light of the billions of stars they contain, also contain dust. This dust is easiest to see and quantify when it overlaps, or is backlit by, another galaxy. Help spot and characterize these rare overlapping galaxy pairs to help reveal how much dust they contain. Overlap Zoo is live! Follow this link to learn more and join the project.

“ Planet Hunters Roman: Extending Citizen Science to Planetary Microlensing” led by Principal Investigator Bernard Gaudi of the Ohio State University. Exoplanets are planets orbiting stars other than our Sun. Their gravity can bend the light that travels around them. This project will invite you to spot exoplanets in data from NASA’s new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope data by the way they bend starlight.

“Space Weather UnderGround: Deploying a low-cost Magnetometer Array with Citizens for Heliophysics Research” led by Principal Investigator Hyunju Connor at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center. Along with sunshine, our Sun produces the solar wind, an unrelenting flow of charged particles. Earth’s protective magnetic field shield deflects most of these particles, but not all, and not during extreme events. Help scientists monitor the subtle disturbances of Earth’s magnetosphere by the solar wind by setting up and monitoring your own magnetometer in Alaska.

“A Citizen Science Initiative for Sonified Plasma Wave Characterization” led by Principal Investigator Lauren Blum of the University Of Colorado, Boulder. “Plasma” is the name given to the ionized gases at the edge of Earth’s magnetosphere. Solar wind, the rain of charged particles that flows out from the Sun, can interact with and generate waves in the plasma. This project will turn data from this dynamic zone into sound signals. You will be invited to listen in to identify waves in the Earth’s magnetosphere.

articles.title: Scientists Discover a Hidden Weakness in Cancer Cells That Could Transform Treatment
articles.dek: A new study reveals a previously overlooked weakness in certain cancer cells that could help researchers refine targeted treatments and reduce harmful side effects.
paragraphs: A new study reveals a previously overlooked weakness in certain cancer cells that could help researchers refine targeted treatments and reduce harmful side effects.

Cancer cells that have lost one safeguard against DNA damage can become dependent on another, an enzyme called Wee1. Drugs that block Wee1 aim to exploit that weakness, but serious side effects are disrupting clinical trials and threatening their adoption in the clinic.

One of the cell’s main safeguards is the tumor-suppressor protein p53, which can halt the cell cycle when DNA damage is detected. In around half of all cancers, p53 is inactive, allowing damaged cells to continue growing. Wee1 provides a second line of defense, acting as a backup brake that prevents cells with damaged DNA from entering cell division. Cancers with mutated p53 rely on this remaining safeguard, making Wee1 an attractive drug target.

A study published in Nature has now revealed that Wee1 also helps healthy cells begin copying their DNA, much earlier in the cell cycle. Researchers from the MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences (LMS), the University of Oxford, and UCL found that this role involves a protein degradation complex, a group of proteins that breaks down molecules needed for DNA replication. Wee1 helps switch off the complex so replication can begin. Without Wee1, the complex remains active, delaying or preventing cells from progressing through the cell cycle.

“We think what’s happening in patients is that when they’re being treated with these Wee1 inhibitors, it’s stopping their normal fast proliferating cells, like you get in the colon and the blood system, from starting to replicate,” says Alexis, head of the Cell Cycle Control group at the LMS. “And so those cells are stuck, unable to generate new cells, and that could be causing some of the toxic side effects.”

The discovery grew out of an effort to test the established understanding of Wee1’s activity early in the cell cycle. The team built a mathematical model based on the scientific literature to predict what would happen when the enzyme was inhibited.

“Wee1 has been very intensely studied in the later stages of the cell cycle, where targeting its activity for cancer treatment makes sense,” says Alexis. “However, the side effects of Wee1 inhibitors in patients were hard to explain based on these functions so we started to wonder if this Wee1 enzyme had some other function that we hadn’t appreciated that could explain these. We wanted to look earlier in the cell cycle to see if there was something we had missed.”

The researchers then tested the model’s predictions in healthy and cancerous cells. Alexis says, “We quickly found out that the model we had based on the literature on Wee1 was wrong because that was not what we saw in cells. What had been missed was an early function of Wee1 that people hadn’t looked at.”

If the side effects are linked to Wee1’s role in controlling the protein degradation complex, the findings could help identify patients most likely to benefit from treatment. The researchers suggest that cancers with reduced activity of this complex may be particularly susceptible to Wee1 inhibitors. That could create a therapeutic window in which lower doses kill cancer cells while limiting damage to healthy cells and reducing side effects.

“We’re also starting to think about if there are different ways we could inhibit Wee1 that get round this early cell cycle function,” says Alexis, “though how this might be achieved is a work in progress.”

The researchers now want to test the work’s predictions further in preclinical models and in patients currently enrolled in Wee1 inhibitor clinical trials. Those tests could help determine whether the newly identified function explains the toxic effects and how that understanding might guide safer treatment.

“Now we’ve uncovered this new function for Wee1, are there other functions that we haven’t appreciated? What else is it doing that we have not seen since we’ve not looked at the right stage?” asks Alexis.
This study was funded by the Medical Research Council and Cancer Research UK.
